input: This passage presents a capital appraisal for a proposed warehouse extension. The appraisal follows the standard discounted cash flow approach, in which the savings expected in future years are discounted back to their value at the present day, so that they can be compared fairly with a cost that is incurred at the outset. The extension itself is an enlargement of the existing warehouse, and the savings arise from the additional capacity it provides. The installed cost of the extension is $784k, and it is expected to generate a net saving of $158k per year over a period of 8 years. Discounting these savings at a discount rate of 8% gives a present value of the savings of $908k. Subtracting the installed cost from the present value of the savings gives a net present value of $124k, which is positive and therefore indicates that the extension is financially worthwhile on the figures presented. It should nevertheless be noted that the savings are estimates provided by the vendor and the utility, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so a considerable degree of uncertainty attaches to the figures and the appraisal should be read with that in mind. The $124k is, in other words, the surplus of the estimated savings over the estimated cost once the timing of both has been taken into account, and it is on that basis that the proposal is put forward for consideration by those responsible for the decision.
target: The warehouse extension has a positive net present value of $124k at the stated figures. The installed cost is $784k, and the expected net saving is $158k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $908k, and the net present value is the present value less the installed cost, $124k. Discounting converts each year's saving to its value at the decision date, so that money arriving later counts for less than money in hand; the net present value is what remains when the installed cost, paid at the start, is set against that discounted stream. A positive value at the stated discount rate means that the savings repay the cost with the required return to spare, on the estimates. The result does not rank the extension against other uses of the same capital, and it says nothing about the savings being achieved in practice. The installed cost is the firmer side of the comparison, a figure that a contract will fix before the saving begins. The result is most exposed to the yearly saving, which is an estimate throughout the life, and to the length of the life itself: a shorter life removes whole years of saving from the discounted stream, and the margin is the first casualty of either change. The finding is a comparison of two estimates. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. The margin is therefore the gap between the estimates as stated, not a measured return: a shortfall in the yearly saving falls directly on the net present value, and the appraisal gives no measured installation from which to bound that shortfall.
